'''Lene Vestergaard Hau''' ({{IPA|da|ˈle̝ːnə ˈvestɐˌkɒˀ ˈhɑw|lang}}; born November 13, 1959) is a Danish [[physicist]] and educator. She is the Mallinckrodt Professor of Physics and of Applied Physics at [[Harvard University]].<ref>{{Cite web| url= https://www.seas.harvard.edu/haulab/lene_vestergaard_hau/lene_vestergaard_hau.htm|title=Lene Vestergaard Hau|website= seas.harvard.edu| publisher= Harvard University| access-date= 2018-10-08}}</ref>  

In 1999, she led a Harvard University team that, by use of a [[Bose–Einstein condensate]], succeeded in [[Slow light|slowing a beam of light]] to about 17 [[metre per second|metres per second]], and, in 2001, was able to stop a beam completely.<ref name= "Lene Hau">{{cite web| website= physicscentral.com| url= http://www.physicscentral.com/explore/people/hau.cfm |title=Lene Hau| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220803185857/https://physicscentral.com/explore/people/hau.cfm |archive-date=2022-08-03}}</ref> Later work based on these experiments led to the transfer of light to matter, then from matter back into light,<ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.seas.harvard.edu/haulab/publications/pdf/Ginsberg-Garner-and-Hau-Nature-445-623-(2007).pdf| title= Coherent control of optical information with matter wave dynamics| website=harvard.edu | publisher= Harvard University}}</ref> a process with important implications for [[quantum encryption]] and [[quantum computing]]. More recent work has focused on novel interactions between [[ultracold atom]]s and [[nanoscopic scale|nanoscopic-scale]] systems. In addition to teaching physics and applied physics, she has taught Energy Science at Harvard,<ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.registrar.fas.harvard.edu/courses-exams/course-catalog/physics-129-energy-science |title= Physics 129. Energy Science| publisher= FAS Registrar's Office, Harvard University |website= registrar.fas.harvard.edu |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20150226080944/http://www.registrar.fas.harvard.edu/courses-exams/course-catalog/physics-129-energy-science |archive-date= 2015-02-26 }}</ref> involving [[photovoltaic cell]]s, [[nuclear power]], [[Battery (electricity)|batteries]], and [[photosynthesis]].

== Early life, family and education ==
{{unreferenced section|date=September 2026}}
Hau was born in [[Vejle]], Denmark. She earned her bachelor's degree in mathematics in 1984 at the [[University of Aarhus]] in Denmark at the age of 24.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Lene Vestergaard Hau - Biography |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Hau/ |access-date=2026-11-04 |website=Maths History |language=en}}</ref> Hau continued her studies there, receiving her master's degree in physics two years later. 

For her doctoral studies in [[quantum mechanics|quantum theory]], Hau worked on ideas similar to those involved in [[Optical fiber|fibre optic]] cables carrying light, but her work involved strings of atoms in a silicon crystal carrying electrons. While working towards her doctorate, Hau spent seven months at [[CERN]], the European Laboratory for Particle Physics near [[Geneva]]. She received her doctorate from the University of Aarhus in 1991 at the age of 32, but by then her research interests had shifted.

== Career ==
In 1991, she joined the [[Rowland Institute for Science]] at [[Cambridge, Massachusetts]] as a scientific staff member, beginning to explore the possibilities of slow light and cold atoms. In 1999, at the age of 40, Hau accepted a two-year appointment as a [[postdoc|postdoctoral fellow]] at Harvard University. Her formalized training is in [[theoretical physics]], but her interest moved to experimental research in an effort to create a new form of [[matter]] known as a [[Bose–Einstein condensate]]. "Hau applied to the [[National Science Foundation]] for funds to make a batch of this condensate but was rejected on the grounds that she was a theorist for whom such experiments would be too difficult to do."<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.news.harvard.edu/gazette/2001/10.25/01-macarthur.html |title=Hau wins MacArthur |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110928063328/http://www.news.harvard.edu/gazette/2001/10.25/01-macarthur.html |archive-date=2011-09-28 }}</ref> Undeterred, she gained alternative funding and became one of the first handful of physicists to create such a condensate. In September 1999, she was appointed the [[Gordon Mckay]] Professor of Applied Physics and Professor of Physics at Harvard.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.thecrimson.com/article/1999/10/13/hau-receives-tenure-physics-professor-slowed/|title=Hau Receives Tenure; Physics Professor Slowed Light &#124; News &#124; The Harvard Crimson|website=www.thecrimson.com}}</ref> She was also awarded tenure in 1999 and is now [[Mallinckrodt]] Professor of Physics and Applied Physics at Harvard. In 2001, she became the first person to stop light completely,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.physicscentral.com/explore/people/hau.cfm|title=Lene Hau|website=www.physicscentral.com}}</ref> using a [[Bose–Einstein condensate]] to achieve this. Since then, she has produced extensive research and new experimental work in [[electromagnetically induced transparency]], various areas of [[quantum physics]], [[photonics]], and has contributed to the development of new quantum devices and novel [[Nanoscopic scale|nanoscale]] applications.

== Qubit transfer ==
Hau and her associates at Harvard University "have demonstrated exquisite control over light and matter in several experiments, but her experiment with 2 condensates is one of the most compelling".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.learner.org/courses/physics/video/video_transcript/unit07_transcript_0.pdf|title=Physics for the 21st century|website=learner.org|access-date=2013-01-21|archive-date=2016-03-04|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304053253/http://www.learner.org/courses/physics/video/video_transcript/unit07_transcript_0.pdf}}</ref> In 2006, they successfully transferred a [[qubit]] from light to a matter wave and back into light, again using [[Bose–Einstein condensate]]s. Details of the experiment are discussed in the February 8, 2007, publication of the journal ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]''.<ref>{{cite journal |url=http://www.nature.com/news/2007/070205/full/news070205-8.html |title=Turning light into matter: Coherent control of optical information with matter wave dynamics|journal=News@nature|doi=10.1038/news070205-8|year=2007|last1=Ball|first1=Philip|pages=news070205–8 |s2cid=122167698|url-access=subscription}}</ref> The experiment relies on the way that, according to quantum mechanics, atoms may behave as waves as well as particles. This enables atoms to do some counterintuitive things, such as passing through two openings at once. Within a Bose–Einstein condensate a light pulse is compressed by a factor of 50&nbsp;million, without losing any of the information stored within it. In this Bose–Einstein condensate, information encoded in a light pulse can be transferred to the atom waves. Because all the atoms move coherently, the information does not dissolve into random noise. The light drives some of the cloud's roughly 1.8&nbsp;million sodium atoms to enter into "quantum superposition" states, with a lower-energy component that stays put and a higher-energy component that travels between the two{{clarify|date=April 2018}} clouds. A second 'control' laser then writes the pulse shape into the atom's wave function. When this control beam is turned off, and the light pulse disappears, the 'matter copy' remains. Prior to this, researchers could not readily control optical information during its journey, except to amplify the signal to avoid fading. This experiment by Hau and her colleagues marked the first successful manipulation of coherent optical information. The new study is "a beautiful demonstration", says [[Irina B. Novikova|Irina Novikova]], a physicist at the [[College of William and Mary]] in Williamsburg, VA. Before this result, she says, light storage was measured in milliseconds. "Here it's fractional seconds. It's a really dramatic time."<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.docstoc.com/docs/56018359/Trapped-in-cloud-of-ultracold-atoms-light-stayed-frozen-for-15-seconds-technique-if-improved-could-lead-to-light-storage-devices(Matter-andamp-Energy)|title=Trapped in cloud of ultracold atoms, light stayed frozen for 1.5 seconds: technique, if improved, could lead to light-storage devices.}}</ref>

Of its potential, Hau said, "While the matter is traveling between the two Bose–Einstein condensates, we can trap it, potentially for minutes, and reshape it – change it – in whatever way we want. This novel form of quantum control could also have applications in the developing fields of quantum information processing and quantum cryptography."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.photonics.com/Article.aspx?AID=28520|title=Light Changed to Matter, Then Stopped and Moved}}</ref>  Of the developmental implications, "This feat, the sharing around of quantum information in light-form and in not just one but two atom-forms, offers great encouragement to those who hope to develop [[quantum computers]]," said [[Jeremy Bloxham]], dean of science in the Faculty of Arts and Sciences.<ref name="Harvard Gazette">{{cite web|url=http://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2008/09/hau-awarded-prestigious-ledlie/ |title=Hau awarded prestigious Ledlie|date=2008-09-25}}</ref> Hau was awarded the [[George Ledlie Prize]] for this work, Harvard's Provost [[Steven Hyman]] noting "her work is path-breaking. Her research blurs the boundaries between basic and applied science, draws on the talent and people of two Schools and several departments, and provides a literally glowing example of how taking daring intellectual risks leads to profound rewards."<ref name="Harvard Gazette"/>

== Cold atoms and nanoscale systems ==
[[File:Nanoblackholes.jpg|thumb|A captured atom is ripped apart as its electron is sucked into the nanotube]]
In 2009, Hau and team laser-cooled clouds of one million rubidium atoms to just a fraction of a degree above [[absolute zero]]. They then launched this millimeter-long atomic cloud towards a suspended carbon nanotube, located some two centimeters away and charged to hundreds of volts. The results were published in 2010, heralding new interactions between cold atoms and nanoscale systems.<ref name=autogenerated1>{{cite journal|title=Field Ionization of Cold Atoms near the Wall of a Single Carbon Nanotube|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=104|issue=13|article-number=133002|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.104.133002|pmid=20481881|pmc=3113630|year=2010|last1=Goodsell|first1=Anne|last2=Ristroph|first2=Trygve|last3=Golovchenko|first3=J. A.|last4=Hau|first4=Lene Vestergaard|bibcode=2010PhRvL.104m3002G|arxiv=1004.2644}}</ref> They observed that most atoms passed by, but approximately 10 per million were inescapably attracted, causing them to dramatically accelerate both in movement and in temperature. "At this point, the speeding atoms separate into an electron and an ion rotating in parallel around the nanowire, completing each orbit in just a few trillionths of a second. The electron eventually gets sucked into the nanotube via quantum tunneling, causing its companion ion to shoot away – repelled by the strong charge of the 300-volt nanotube – at a speed of roughly 26&nbsp;kilometers per second, or 59,000&nbsp;miles per hour."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2010/04/100406125716.htm|title=Cold atoms and nanotubes come together in an atomic 'black hole'|website=ScienceDaily}}</ref> Atoms can rapidly disintegrate, without having to collide with each other, in this experiment. The team notes that this effect is not produced by gravity in [[black hole]]s, as calculated for black holes in space, but by the high electrical charge in the nanotube. The experiment combines nanotechnology with cold atoms to demonstrate a new type of high-resolution, single-atom, chip-integrated detector that may ultimately resolve fringes from the interference of matter waves. The scientists also foresee a range of single-atom, fundamental studies made possible by their setup.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Physics – Ionizing atoms with a nanotube|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=104|issue=13|article-number = 133002|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.104.133002|pmid=20481881|pmc=3113630|year=2010|last1=Goodsell|first1=Anne|last2=Ristroph|first2=Trygve|last3=Golovchenko|first3=J. A|last4=Hau|first4=Lene Vestergaard|arxiv=1004.2644|bibcode=2010PhRvL.104m3002G}}</ref>
